ANIME: ITS BRIEF
Close The Brief
Last Launch From The Roof
A practice brief for Anime: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Last Launch From The Roof
The Spillway Walk

Dubbing an existing scene, an apprentice glider pilot tells her rival on the academy roof that she’s leaving tomorrow, and the lines have to fit mouths already drawn.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A dubbing booth. On the screen, a flight academy’s rooftop at sunset, gliders tied down in a rising wind; the animation is finished and every line must land on the lip movements already in it. In the story, she has just failed her final flight and has been sent home.
The Two Of You
Rivals since their first day, who have never once admitted they’re friends.
You Play
Haru, an apprentice pilot of seventeen, who laughs when she’s about to cry.
You Speak To
The voice speaks to Rin, her rival, already recorded on the track; the actor plays against his lines in the headphones.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. The take weighs execution and connection more and draws on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
Dense Text, Exact: A lot of words, or difficult ones, delivered fluently and at speed: jargon, argument or deduction as second nature. The take weighs execution and interpretation more and draws on your memory and focus. Learning the lines: fluency at speed is the lines learned past knowing them.
Dubbing asks for emotional truth sized to the drawn image while the timing fits mouth movements that already exist. From the genre’s research, mostly at low confidence.
What You Want
Say goodbye without letting him see it matters.
What’s In The Way
He won’t accept it, and every line has to fit a mouth that opens and closes on the picture’s timing, not hers.
WHERE IT TURNS
She jokes about the failed landing, fitting each quip to the drawn laugh. (Comic)
He says she’s the best pilot in the year, and her answer comes out too fast for the flaps; she has to find it again. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
She admits she wanted to fly against him forever, as the drawn sun goes down. (Lyric)

2 changes of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal counts complete at 50% in a beat, and at up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, 8% more in one held two ways. Bravado, a crack she has to fit back into the picture, then the plain admission.

WHAT LAST LAUNCH FROM THE ROOF ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Built On It. Every line fits mouth movements that already exist, so where each word falls is fixed by the picture.
Playing Off The Partner: Some
Vocal Demand: Much. The laugh that turns to tears is carried by the voice alone, and the volume rises with the wind on the track.
Tone: comic to grave to lyric, 2 transitions to play. Bravado, a crack she has to fit back into the picture, then the plain admission.
Techniques It Asks: Voice-Over. A dub recorded alone at a microphone, synced to finished animation and his recorded lines.
It Only Takes: Set. The animation is finished, so every line has to land where the drawn lips already move. It can only be played set, the same way every time.

title: Episode Two Hundred
text:

TRAGICOMEDY: ITS BRIEF
Close The Brief
Episode Two Hundred
A practice brief for Tragicomedy: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Three Minutes
Episode Two Hundred

Recording alone, a radio host makes the last episode of the comedy show she made with her late partner for eleven years, playing both halves of their oldest running bit.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A small studio at a community radio station on a Sunday night. For eleven years Bea and Lou made a weekly comedy show for the station; Lou died in the summer, and the station asked Bea for one last episode for the listeners. Their oldest bit was an argument between two neighbors over a fence, Bea as one and Lou as the other. Tonight she plays both. Recorded alone at a microphone, live to tape, as the episode goes out.
The Two Of You
Partners on air for eleven years and friends for thirty; off the air they argued about everything, on it only about the fence.
You Play
Bea Rourke, sixty-two, quick, dry and set on getting through it without the listeners hearing her cry.
You Speak To
No reader: the voice speaks to the listeners, and in the bit, as each neighbor, to the other.
The Genre Asks
Comic Rhythm: Setup and payoff: cues picked up, pauses placed, the laugh landing where the timing puts it. The take weighs responsiveness and execution more and draws on your adaptability and focus. Rehearsing on your feet: timing lives in the exchange and is found by playing it through.
Played Straight: Meant completely: the feeling played with full conviction, never winked at, however large or strange the material. The take weighs believability and connection more and draws on your emotional depth and presence. The breakdown and the lines: believing it starts with knowing exactly what your character wants and why it matters to them.
Tone shifting between the serious and the comic, often within a scene. From the genre’s research, mostly at low confidence.
What You Want
Give the listeners the show Lou would have wanted, and get to the end of it.
What’s In The Way
The bit was built for two voices and two kinds of timing, Lou’s half is the funnier, and every line of it is his.
WHERE IT TURNS
The show’s opening as always: the theme hummed, the weather, and a complaint about the station’s coffee. (Comic)
She says, briefly and without fuss, that Lou won’t be on tonight. (Grave)
The fence bit: both neighbors in both voices, faster and faster, a double act’s timing from one mouth. (Comic)
In Lou’s voice, his neighbor says the line he always ended on, and she can’t answer it in her own. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
She thanks the listeners for eleven years and signs off the way the two of them always did, alone. (Lyric and Comic, held at once)

4 changes of tone between beats and 2 beats held two ways. Rehearsal counts complete at 50% in a beat, and at up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, 8% more in one held two ways. The usual opening, a plain word about Lou, the bit at full speed, the line she can’t answer, then the sign-off.

WHAT EPISODE TWO HUNDRED ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Built On It. A double act’s timing played by one voice: each switch between the neighbors has to land as fast as Lou would have answered.
Vocal Demand: Built On It. Two neighbors from one mouth, her own voice and Lou’s character kept apart, live to tape, with no second take.
Tone: comic to grave to lyric, 4 transitions to play. The usual opening, a plain word about Lou, the bit at full speed, the line she can’t answer, then the sign-off.
Techniques It Asks: Comedy, Character Work. Comedy carries the bit’s timing, and it has to be as funny for the listeners as it always was. Character work carries Lou’s neighbor, a voice and a rhythm that were his and are hers to keep tonight.

text:

TOKUSATSU: ITS BRIEF
Close The Brief
The Voice In The Armor
A practice brief for Tokusatsu: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
The Observation Tower
The Voice In The Armor

An actor dubs his own armored hero’s finale, fitting every cry, breath and line to a suit performer’s finished fight footage, as the hero chooses to spare his oldest rival.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A dubbing studio. On the screen, the series’ final fight, filmed months ago: a suit performer in the hero’s armor and another in the rival’s black armor, on a miniature rooftop set under practical sparks. In tokusatsu the masked hero’s lines are recorded afterward, usually by the actor who plays him unmasked, to the suit performer’s movements, so the voice has to fit a body it doesn’t own. In the story, the hero has his rival beaten and won’t strike the last blow.
The Two Of You
Hero and rival were cadets in the same academy before the rival went over to the other side, and have fought each other for fifty episodes.
You Play
Sota Hanabusa, twenty-four, who becomes the armored hero Hoshikage, voiced in armor by the actor who plays him unmasked.
You Speak To
The voice speaks to Jin, the rival, whose lines are already on the track; the actor plays against them in the headphones and to the suit on the screen.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. The take weighs execution and connection more and draws on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
Command Of The Frame: Status and threat carried in the body and the look more than the words: the person everyone in the room watches. The take weighs connection and execution more and draws on your presence and physical expression. Rehearsing on your feet: status is found standing, in how little you need to move.
Suit actors act through body language in full costume, voices dubbed later. From the genre’s research, mostly at low confidence.
What You Want
Get Jin to stand down and come home without striking the last blow.
What’s In The Way
Jin begs him to finish it, and every word has to land inside a suited body’s movements that were fixed months ago.
WHERE IT TURNS
The transformation call, over the footage of the armor locking on, sized to the pose and held to the last spark. (Grave)
The last exchange of blows, every strike and breath fitted to the suit performer’s moves on the screen. (Grave)
On the screen the hero lowers his fist, and he tells Jin he won’t, keeping the voice steady inside a body still heaving. (Lyric and Grave, held at once)
Jin asks why, and the hero answers with the old cadet joke only the two of them know. (Comic and Lyric, held at once)

2 changes of tone between beats and 2 beats held two ways. Rehearsal counts complete at 50% in a beat, and at up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, 8% more in one held two ways. A transformation called at full size, a fight in breath and effort, mercy spoken inside a heaving body, then a joke between two old cadets.

WHAT THE VOICE IN THE ARMOR ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Built On It. Every cry, breath and line is fitted to a suit performer’s movements already on the screen, so where each sound falls is fixed by the picture.
Physical Work: Some
Playing Off The Partner: Some
Vocal Demand: Built On It. The call, the efforts of the fight and the quiet mercy are all the voice has, carried from a full-voiced cry to a near whisper inside one take.
Tone: grave to lyric to comic, 2 transitions to play. A transformation called at full size, a fight in breath and effort, mercy spoken inside a heaving body, then a joke between two old cadets.
Techniques It Asks: Voice-Over. Post-synced voice work recorded alone at a microphone to finished footage and a rival already on the track, with the body’s effort put into breath and voice.
It Only Takes: Set. The footage is finished and the suit’s moves are fixed, so every sound has to land where the body already moves. It can only be played set, the same way every time.
